plan.contextChunk: This figure is a coordinate plane carrying four straight lines, each in a different color with arrowheads on both ends and tagged with a Roman numeral. The horizontal axis is labeled x and numbered from -7 to 7, the vertical axis is labeled y and numbered from -5 to 5, and a light gray unit grid fills the plotting region. Line I is orange and by far the steepest, rising from below the x-axis at the lower left and exiting through the top of the grid just right of the y-axis, where its label sits. Line II is light blue and the shallowest, entering at the left near x equal to -6.5 on the x-axis, crossing the y-axis at 3, and climbing to about x equal to 4, y equal to 5. Line III is teal, crossing the y-axis at -3 and the x-axis near x equal to 1.5 before rising to that same upper right region. Line IV is dark blue and the only line with a negative slope, entering at the upper left, crossing the y-axis at 3, and descending to roughly x equal to 4, y equal to -4.5. Color and numeral identify the lines, leaving steepness and direction as the properties to read off. The plot supports an exercise in pairing four given linear equations with the correct lines.

interactionPlan.concept: A line's equation y = mx + b can be matched to its graph by reading b as the y-intercept and m as the signed rise-over-run that controls direction and steepness.

interactions.label: Slope m
interactions.teaches: Changing m shows that positive slopes rise left to right, negative slopes fall left to right, and larger absolute values make the line visually steeper

interactions.label: y-intercept b
interactions.teaches: Changing b shows that the whole line shifts up or down while keeping the same slope, and that b is read where the line crosses the y-axis
Selecting one of lines I-IV isolates its intercept and rise-over-run so the learner can connect the visual graph to the matching equation

demo_steps.title: Start with the y-intercept
demo_steps.narration: Set b = 3 and notice that lines I, II, and IV all cross the y-axis at the same point. The y-intercept narrows the choices, but it does not identify the slope by itself.

demo_steps.title: Use slope to separate shared intercepts
demo_steps.narration: With b fixed at 3, changing m rotates the candidate line around the point (0, 3). A shallow positive slope matches II, a steep positive slope matches I, and a steep negative slope matches IV.

demo_steps.title: Same slope, different intercept
demo_steps.narration: Keep the steep positive slope and lower b from 3 to -3. The candidate line shifts down to match III, showing that parallel lines can have the same slope but different y-intercepts.

demo_steps.title: Click to read rise over run
demo_steps.narration: Click any labeled line to display its rise-over-run triangle. The triangle turns the line's steepness into the numerical slope used in y = mx + b.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: To match a linear equation to a graph, first find where the line crosses the y-axis for b, then use the line's signed rise-over-run for m.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the original plot as a clean coordinate grid from about x = -7 to 7 and y = -5 to 5 with light gray unit squares and darker black axes through the origin. Draw four colored double-arrowed lines: I orange, steep positive, approximately y = 2x + 3; II light blue, shallow positive, approximately y = 0.5x + 3; III teal, steep positive, approximately y = 2x - 3; IV dark blue, steep negative, approximately y = -2x + 3. Place the Roman numeral labels near the same line ends as in the source image. Overlay the learner's candidate line as a dashed contrasting line controlled by m and b. When a line is clicked, dim the other lines slightly and draw a small right-triangle rise/run marker along the selected line, using upward rise for positive slopes and downward rise for negative slopes.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for slope; the learner changes m in a candidate line, a movable line rotates around its y-intercept, and the connection between slope sign, steepness, and matching one of lines I-IV becomes clear.
- Slider for y-intercept; the learner shifts the candidate line up and down, its crossing on the y-axis updates, and the role of b in distinguishing lines with similar direction becomes clear.

authoredContext:
Match each equation of the linear functions with one of the lines in the figure.

A coordinate plane with x and y axes ranging from -7 to 7 and -5 to 5 respectively. Four lines, labeled I (orange), II (light blue), III (teal), and IV (dark blue), are shown. Line I and Line IV intersect at (0, 3). Line III and Line IV intersect at (1.5, 0). Line II and Line III intersect at (4, 5). Lines I, II, and III have positive slopes, while Line IV has a negative slope.

discrepancies: the generated graph uses a non-square plotting aspect ratio, so one x-unit is visibly narrower than one y-unit; the source has square grid cells and therefore more faithful visual slopes
a dashed purple candidate line is drawn by default on top of line II, but the source figure contains only the four solid colored lines I–IV
the extra candidate line and right-side instructional UI change the default static appearance from the source's clean coordinate-plane figure
the top labels I and II are placed very close to the top border/arrowheads compared with the source, where they sit more cleanly above the corresponding lines
evaluation.notes: The four lines, colors, intercepts, arrows, axes, and labels are mostly correct, but the non-square grid and default purple overlay prevent it from being a clean drop-in match for the source.
action_items: Force equal x/y unit scaling so the grid cells are square and the visual slopes match the source figure.
Hide the dashed purple candidate line in the default state, or make it appear only after the user activates an interaction.
Move the I and II labels slightly away from the top border and arrowheads to better match the source label placement.
Keep the static default view focused on the four source lines, with explanatory UI and rise/run annotations appearing only through interaction.

feedback.rationale: The concept and plan are correct, but the remaining issues are concrete rendering/default-state fixes such as square scaling, hiding the extra overlay, and adjusting label placement.

discrepancies: the generated figure adds a large instructional control panel and interactive narration beside the graph, so the default composition is not a clean standalone reproduction of the static textbook image

line labels use a bold sans-serif style with white halos and slightly different placement from the source, especially the top labels I and II, which are pushed above the grid rather than sitting close to the arrow tips as in the source
the line strokes and arrowheads are somewhat thinner/smoother and more stylized than the source, with arrowheads less similar to the textbook's simple triangular tips
the source has a compact cropped graph-only layout, while the generated graph is shifted left and scaled down because of the side UI
evaluation.notes: The graph geometry, four colored lines, coordinates, axes, grid, and labels are highly accurate, but the added side UI and slightly altered label/stroke styling make it less like a direct static replacement.
action_items: Offer a default static mode or hide/collapse the side control panel initially so the graph alone more closely matches the source image.
Adjust label placement and styling to better match the source: smaller/plain labels positioned near the line arrowheads without large white halos.
Tune line widths and arrowhead shapes to more closely resemble the textbook's simple straight colored segments with triangular arrow tips.
